content: The patient with peptic ulcer disease often presents in significant distress due to severe abdominal pain. In cases of perforated peptic ulcer disease, the patient typically exhibits a classic triad of symptoms: severe tenderness in the epigastric region, tachycardia, and abdominal rigidity. Within the next 2 to 12 hours, the patient may develop tenderness in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen along with persistent abdominal rigidity. Beyond 12 hours, the clinical picture may progress to include abdominal distension, hypotension, fever (pyrexia), and acute circulatory collapse. On physical examination: Appearance of the Patient: The patient generally appears to be in severe distress due to intense abdominal pain. Vital Signs: In the early stages of peptic ulcer disease, vital signs are typically normal. However, in cases of perforation, the following changes may be observed: Tachycardia with a regular pulse. A weak pulse. Low blood pressure with a normal pulse pressure. High-grade fever, which is a late finding in the progression of peptic ulcer perforation. Skin: Pallor is often noted in patients presenting with hematemesis (vomiting blood) and melena (black, tarry stools). For example, the hand of a patient with severe anemia may appear significantly paler compared to someone without anemia. HEENT (Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat): Pallor can be observed on the lower conjunctiva. Lungs: Bilateral vesicular breath sounds are normal. Heart: The heart sounds S1 and S2 are normal, with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops detected.
